issues: Misquote: the correction says Montulli 'later called [it] the one gotcha'. The NYT (2001) has: ''That's the one 'gotcha' we had,'' he recalls with chagrin. The correction now quotes it exactly. The NYT source quote is extended to cover it.

Verdict: the inventor's stated design goal was the opposite of the claim. It was a mechanism 'that didn't allow for cross site tracking', and he opposed a per-browser unique ID because it 'could be used to track a user at every website'. The NYT independently says third-party cookies were 'precisely the kind of tracking mechanism Mr. Montulli had tried to prevent'. The claim ('invented to track people across the web') is therefore FALSE rather than MISLEADING.

fieldFixes.correction: Lou Montulli designed the cookie at Netscape in 1994 as a per-site memory (a session identifier, a username, a shopping cart). He says he opposed the idea then circulating, a unique identifier for every browser, because it 'could be used to track a user at every website'. His goal was a mechanism 'that didn't allow for cross site tracking'. Cross-site tracking through third-party cookies was an unforeseen consequence: 'That's the one "gotcha" we had,' he told The New York Times in 2001. He also defended leaving third-party cookies enabled, on the ground that trackers would otherwise use less visible methods.

issues: Conflation: the correction says that 'when Internet Explorer 10 sent it by default, Microsoft later conceded that sites could argue' the signal did not reflect user preference. The 2015 Microsoft post says this about its NEW browsers ('websites that receive a DNT signal from the new browsers could argue...'), as the reason for dropping the default going forward. About IE10 it says only that the default 'was welcomed by many, others voiced concerns'. The correction now keeps the two apart.

The 'no US law' claim was unsourced. Support is added: the GPC FAQ records that the California Attorney General, in the CCPA Final Statement of Reasons, 'determined that the AG could not require businesses to comply with DNT requests'.

The correction was incomplete outside the US. On 24 August 2023 the Landgericht Berlin (vzbv v. LinkedIn, 16 O 420/19, not final when announced) held that 'A DNT signal represents a valid objection' under the GDPR. This does not make DNT a law, so the verdict FALSE stands. But the absolute 'recipients decided what the signal meant' no longer holds everywhere. A sourced sentence is added.
Checked OK: W3C Note of 17 January 2019 ('The working group has therefore decided to conclude its work'). The quote is FOUND. The Microsoft quote is FOUND, dated 3 April 2015.

fieldFixes.correction: DNT was a voluntary HTTP header, not a law. The W3C never finished it as a standard: in January 2019 the working group concluded its work for lack of deployment. No US law required sites to honour it. When drafting the CCPA regulations, California's attorney general concluded he could not require businesses to comply with DNT requests. In practice recipients decided what the signal meant. When Microsoft turned DNT on by default in Internet Explorer 10, 'others voiced concerns'. In 2015 Microsoft dropped the default, conceding that otherwise websites receiving the signal from its new browsers 'could argue that it doesn't reflect the users' preference, and therefore, choose not to honor it'. The one later legal twist came in Europe. In 2023 a Berlin regional court, in a judgment not final when announced, held that a DNT signal is a valid objection under the GDPR. That was a reading of the GDPR, not a DNT law.

issues: Overstated for P3P as a whole. 'Had no way to propose terms' is true of the final P3P 1.0 Recommendation (2002), whose text contains neither 'proposal' nor 'negotiat'. It is not true of P3P's early design. The W3C Working Draft of 2 July 1998 let a user agent that disliked a site's proposal 'Return a Proposal of its own', a counter-proposal, and said P3P provided for 'a user agent and service to automatically negotiate and to come to an agreement satisfactory to both parties'. P3P author Lorrie Cranor later wrote that 'The negotiation protocol was not included in the final specification'. This matters for the IEEE 7012 story: person-side proposals were designed into P3P and then dropped. The correction and sources are updated.

Checked OK: the P3P 1.0 abstract quote (the site expresses its practices; user agents interpret them) and Cranor's blog (browsers compare policies with 'each user's privacy settings' and 'could alert the user, block cookies') are both verbatim.

fieldFixes.correction: In the P3P 1.0 standard (W3C Recommendation, 2002) the website wrote the machine-readable policy. The person only configured preferences in their browser, which compared the site's policy with them and could alert the user or block cookies. The person could accept or refuse a site's stated practices but had no way to propose terms. Early drafts had gone further: a 1998 working draft let the user's agent 'Return a Proposal of its own'. As P3P co-author Lorrie Cranor later wrote, 'The negotiation protocol was not included in the final specification.' That is the direction IEEE 7012 reverses, with the person proffering the terms.
